title: Lester stranded in Virginia: taking the rap and hoboing home
summary: Phillips tells how Blue Devils members were stranded in Virginia, Lester took the blame for a friend's whiskey selling and nearly got put on a chain gang, then rode the rails home to his wife Beatrice, married in 1930.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Well, he joined us, and then he went to... A lot of what they're saying there is wrong. He didn't go back to Minneapolis no more after he left... I mean, to work... He might have went there to play with Basie or somebody. But when he left Minneapolis with the Blue Devils Band, Kansas City, that's where he was. When the band broke
Phillips - 106

up out in Staunton, Virginia, they all hoboed and got back to Kansas City. They made it back there. So while I was in Kansas City, we were looking for a tenor player. So he happened to be there, and he came on. He said, "Yeah, man. I'm broke. I ain't got no money, ain't got no clothes, ain't got nothin'. Because one of the guys in the band, Sam Allen, had let him have one of his suits to wear. Sam's dead now; he died last Christmas. Not that we were going to see him go. We took him down, got him clothes, got him lookin' good -- like we was, you know. So he told us what a rough time he had. He said, "Rough times." They got out there and got stranded, and he messed around with some cat that used to be on Old Man Young's show, driving a car... He bought an automobile and he had this guy chauffeuring for him. So he ran into this guy in Virginia, and this guy, they caught him for selling whiskey.
The guy that Lester was with.

Yeah, knew him. I knew the cat, too. He used to drive on the show, on this minstrel show. So he told Les, said, "Les, you ain't got no record, ain't got nothin'. I want you to go up and stand for this for me." Les, he went up there and stood up for that man. They said they had a hell of a hard time to try to keep them from sending him on a chain gang.
Who had a hard time trying to keep him from getting sent
Phillips - 107
on a chain gang?
The guys in the band.
In the Blue Devils Band.
Yeah, the Blue Devils.
This guy sent him to go up to the court for him?
Yeah. See, he was bullshittin' Les. Les didn't know nothin' about nothin' like that too much...
Exactly what did he tell him to do?
He told him to say he was the man, because they wasn't goin' to do nothin' to him. This guy, they caught him sellin' whiskey. See, this was before Prohibition.
How did the court believe that Lester had anything to do with it?
Well, they...
Even if he told them, didn't they catch the other guy doing it?

Yeah, but you know, in Virginia in them times they didn't care anything about a black man. You know what I mean? They'd give him hell. So Les said he told them, 'I don't know...' But anyway, Les still stuck to it that he did it, that it was him. See, he went up front. He took this rap for the guy.
Even though they did catch the other guy.
Oh, they caught the other guy, but he took the rap.
Phillips - 108
But even the guys who arrested the other fellow, they didn't disagree when Lester said that he did it?

I don't know exactly the whole situation of it. But I know they said they had a hell of a time to keep him from going on the chain gang. They was going to put him on a chain gang for 60 days in Virginia. That's the way it was. And he said he finally got out it. He said, when he got out of it, about five or six of them got out of there and caught a train, and hoboed back to Kansas City. You know, you could do that in them days. They didn't bother you too much. You could get on a train and the policemen didn't bother you if you were hoboin'. You could do that.

Then he came back. Well, he was flat broke, didn't have nothin', you know what I mean? Plus, he had a wife in Kansas City.
Lester already had a wife.
Yeah. She was named Beatrice.
When did he first get married?
He married her in 1930.
She was in Kansas City?
